title.zh: 佐治亚州的地理与五大地区

clips.send: Brasstown Bald. 4,784 ft (1,458 m) — the roof of Georgia. On a clear day you can see four states from the tower on top: Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina and South Carolina.
clips.text: Brasstown Bald. 4,784 ft (1,458 m) — the roof of Georgia. On a clear day you can see four states from the tower on top: Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina and South Carolina.

clips.send: Blue Ridge. Georgia’s tallest mountains. Location: the northeast corner. Brasstown Bald (4,784 ft / 1,458 m) is the highest point in Georgia; the Appalachian Trail starts at Springer Mountain. Climate: the coolest region, with some snow in winter and the most rain in the state — up to about 70–80 inches a year. Agriculture: apples (Ellijay), cattle, poultry and hardwood forests on steep slopes. Economy: tourism (hiking, rafting, Tallulah Gorge), timber — and the 1829 gold rush at Dahlonega.

clips.send: Appalachian Plateau. Flat-topped mountains and deep canyons. Location: the tiny far-northwest corner — Lookout Mountain and Sand Mountain. It is Georgia’s smallest region. Climate: cool, with plenty of rain; streams have carved deep canyons such as Cloudland Canyon. Agriculture: limited — thin, rocky soil on the plateau tops. Economy: tourism (canyons, caves, waterfalls); coal and iron ore were once mined here.

clips.send: Chattahoochee River. Atlanta’s water supply and part of the Alabama border. About 430 miles from the Blue Ridge to the Florida line. Lake Lanier stores its water for metro Atlanta; Columbus grew at its Fall Line falls; it forms much of the Georgia–Alabama border.

clips.send: Cloudland Canyon. Canyons cut into Lookout Mountain. Sitton Gulch Creek carved canyons hundreds of feet deep into the edge of the plateau, with waterfalls you can hike to.
clips.text: Cloudland Canyon. Canyons cut into Lookout Mountain. Sitton Gulch Creek carved canyons hundreds of feet deep into the edge of the plateau, with waterfalls you can hike to.

clips.send: Piedmont. Rolling hills and red clay. Location: from the mountains down to the Fall Line — about a third of Georgia. “Piedmont” means “foot of the mountains.” Climate: hot summers, mild winters, about 50 inches of rain. Rolling hills of red clay (colored by iron) and granite such as Stone Mountain. Agriculture: poultry (Gainesville calls itself the “Poultry Capital of the World”), cattle, dairy, timber; it was cotton country in the 1800s. Economy: the most people and jobs — Atlanta, Athens and the busy Hartsfield-Jackson airport; business, transportation, government and universities.

clips.send: Tallulah Gorge. A gorge almost 1,000 ft deep. The Tallulah River cut this gorge about 2 miles long. In 1970 Karl Wallenda walked across it on a tightrope.
clips.text: Tallulah Gorge. A gorge almost 1,000 ft deep. The Tallulah River cut this gorge about 2 miles long. In 1970 Karl Wallenda walked across it on a tightrope.

clips.send: Valley and Ridge. Ridges and fertile valleys side by side. Location: the northwest, between the Appalachian Plateau and the Blue Ridge. Long ridges such as Taylor Ridge run southwest–northeast with valleys between. Climate: mild — cooler than the south, with about 50–55 inches of rain. Agriculture: grain, hay, cattle, poultry and dairy in the limestone valleys. Economy: manufacturing — Dalton is called the “Carpet Capital of the World”; Rome grew where two rivers meet to form the Coosa.

clips.send: Cumberland Island. Georgia’s largest barrier island. About 17 miles long, with wild horses, dunes and live-oak forest. It is protected by the National Park Service.
clips.text: Cumberland Island. Georgia’s largest barrier island. About 17 miles long, with wild horses, dunes and live-oak forest. It is protected by the National Park Service.

clips.send: Appalachian Mountains (Springer Mtn.). The southern end of a 1,500-mile mountain chain. The Appalachians cover the Blue Ridge, Valley and Ridge and Appalachian Plateau. Mountains block easy travel, so north Georgia was settled later — and its rain feeds rivers for the whole state.

clips.send: 塔卢拉峡谷。一条近 1,000 英尺深的峡谷。塔卢拉河切出了这条长约 2 英里的峡谷。1970 年，走钢丝演员卡尔·瓦伦达从峡谷上空走了过去。
clips.text: 塔卢拉峡谷. 一条近 1,000 英尺深的峡谷. 塔卢拉河切出了这条长约 2 英里的峡谷。1970 年，走钢丝演员卡尔·瓦伦达从峡谷上空走了过去。

clips.send: 岭谷区。山岭与肥沃的谷地交替排列。位置：西北部，夹在阿巴拉契亚高原和蓝岭之间。泰勒岭等长长的山岭呈西南、东北走向，中间是谷地。 气候：温和，比南部凉爽，年降水约 50到55 英寸。 农业：石灰岩谷地里种粮食和牧草，养牛、家禽和奶牛。 经济：制造业——多尔顿被称为“世界地毯之都”；罗马市位于两条河汇成库萨河的地方。
clips.text: 岭谷区. 山岭与肥沃的谷地交替排列. 位置：西北部，夹在阿巴拉契亚高原和蓝岭之间。泰勒岭等长长的山岭呈西南—东北走向，中间是谷地。 气候：温和，比南部凉爽，年降水约 50～55 英寸。 农业：石灰岩谷地里种粮食和牧草，养牛、家禽和奶牛。 经济：制造业——多尔顿被称为“世界地毯之都”；罗马市位于两条河汇成库萨河的地方。

clips.send: 沿海平原。平坦的农田、松林和海岸。位置：瀑布线以南的全部地区，约占全州五分之三。地势平坦、土壤多沙，远古时曾在海底。 气候：最炎热、生长季最长；夏季潮湿，靠近海岸时可能遭遇飓风。 农业：内沿海平原是佐治亚州的农业带——花生（约占全美产量的一半）、棉花、山核桃、维达利亚洋葱、桃子和蓝莓。 经济：农业，松林供造纸和木材，萨凡纳港和不伦瑞克港，奥克弗诺基沼泽和堰洲岛吸引游客。

clips.send: 云地峡谷。切入瞭望山的峡谷。西顿峡溪在高原边缘切出数百英尺深的峡谷，徒步就能到达瀑布。
clips.text: 云地峡谷. 切入瞭望山的峡谷. 西顿峡溪在高原边缘切出数百英尺深的峡谷，徒步就能到达瀑布。

clips.send: 蓝岭山区。佐治亚州最高的山。位置：东北角。布拉斯敦秃山（4,784 英尺，1,458 米）是佐治亚州最高点；阿巴拉契亚步道从斯普林格山出发。 气候：最凉爽的地区，冬季有时下雪，降水全州最多——每年可达约 70到80 英寸。 农业：苹果（埃利杰）、牛、家禽，陡坡上是阔叶林。 经济：旅游（徒步、漂流、塔卢拉峡谷）、木材——1829 年达洛尼加还掀起过淘金热。

clips.send: 阿巴拉契亚高原。平顶山和深峡谷。位置：西北角的一小块——瞭望山和沙山。它是佐治亚州面积最小的地区。 气候：凉爽多雨；溪流切出了云地峡谷等深谷。 农业：有限——高原顶部土层薄、石头多。 经济：旅游（峡谷、洞穴、瀑布）；这里过去开采过煤和铁矿石。

clips.send: 查塔胡奇河。亚特兰大的水源，也是与阿拉巴马州边界的一部分。从蓝岭到佛罗里达州边界，全长约 430 英里。拉尼尔湖为大亚特兰大储水；哥伦布在它的瀑布线急流处兴起；它构成了佐治亚州与阿拉巴马州边界的大部分。

clips.send: 阿巴拉契亚山脉（斯普林格山）。一条约 1,500 英里长山脉的南端。阿巴拉契亚山脉覆盖蓝岭、岭谷区和阿巴拉契亚高原。山地阻碍交通，所以北佐治亚开发得较晚——但这里的雨水为全州的河流提供了源头。

clips.send: 皮德蒙特高原。起伏的丘陵和红土。位置：从山区一直到瀑布线，约占全州三分之一。“皮德蒙特”的意思是“山脚”。 气候：夏热冬温，年降水约 50 英寸。起伏的丘陵上是红土（含铁），还有石山这样的花岗岩。 农业：家禽（盖恩斯维尔自称“世界家禽之都”）、牛、奶牛、木材；19 世纪这里是产棉区。 经济：人口和工作岗位最多——亚特兰大、雅典市和繁忙的哈茨菲尔德-杰克逊机场；商业、交通、政府和大学。

clips.send: 布拉斯敦秃山。4,784 英尺（1,458 米）——佐治亚之巅。天气晴朗时，从山顶观景塔能望见四个州：佐治亚、田纳西、北卡罗来纳和南卡罗来纳。
